title: Mormonism and the Pacific World
description: Religions move across real and imagined boundaries. What can Mormonisms historical movement across the Pacific world tell us about religion? About its interconnectedness with politics, empires, and ideas about race, ethnicity, and gender? This course pursues these questions, and more, through a rigorous engagement with existing scholarship, class discussion, guest speakers, and primary research projects designed to examine religions propensity both to migrate and to become rooted (and transformed) in new global spaces.

title: The Novels of Neal Stephenson: Science, Literature, Ethics
description: Neal Stephenson may be best known for his 1992 novel, Snow Crash, which was inspirational to many pioneers of Silicon Valley. This course explores the interface of the novel with the history of science across the Stephensons work. We will ask a number of questions about the power of literary narrative to address the ethical questions raised by the development of technology; and about the power of narrative to not only represent the world but to elaborate new forms of life on the basis of technological advancements.

title: Studies of Non-Violence
description: The doctrine of nonviolence is applicable across South Asian Religious Traditions. Students will be introduced to the background of nonviolence and its contemporary expressions. This course is divided into two main parts: theoretical aspects of nonviolence and how nonviolence is applied across cultures to problems of the environment and social justice. Practical aspects of nonviolence will merge philosophies of East and West, explaining nonviolence in daily lives.

title: Writing Nature from the Sublime to the Anthropocene
description: Explores different ways that nature-writing has been conceptualized and practiced (whether in essayistic, poetic, or philosophical modes). Beginning with the 18th-century concept of the Sublime and ending with the Anthropocene (the age we are thought to be living in now), our discussions will move through several key epochs in order to consider how the cultural imagination has shapedand has been shaped byshifting understandings of the relationship between humans and nature. Ultimately, we will invite all of these texts to address themselves to us in our own ecologically fraught moment, asking: what does it mean to engage in nature-writing when facing a natural world whose fate often seems to have already been written?

title: On Experience: Religion, Philosophy, Art
description: Explores different constructions of the concept of experience. Examines how experience has been conceptualized as a form of knowledge in the writings of philosophers, pursued as a mean of self-transformation in the religious practice of mystics, and fashioned in the work of artists.

title: American Religious Lives
description: Examines religion in the U.S. through biography. Traces how religion figures in American lives across time and space, how we narrate those biographies, and what the changing ways we tell these stories might reveal about national cultures. From the obscure to the celebrity, we'll probe how religion intersects with other dimensions of identity and experience in the making of American lives.

title: Introduction to South Asian Traditions
description: This introductory course aims to provide an outline of diverse traditions and cultures that encompasses modern South Asia. Beginning with Hinduism, Jainism, Buddhism, and Sikhism that originated in the Indian subcontinent, the course will then examine Islam and Christianity in shaping Indian civilization. Drawing on texts, narratives, cultures and religious practices, the major areas of explorations will be socio-religious debates on gender and devotion, tradition and modernity. Also considers the various aspects of convergence or divergence amongst the traditions that makeup South Asia.

title: Mission Santa Barbara: History and Society
description: This course examines the art, architecture, and history of Mission Santa Barbara, with an emphasis on using primary sources (written, visual, and archaeological) to understand different ways in which a religious institution and civic community can interact.

title: Morality Critics: Nietzsche, Wittgenstein, Heidegger
description: Considers a set of philosophical texts which call into question moral philosophy as it is sometimes practiced. Starting with Nietzsche, and then turning to Wittgenstein and Martin Heidegger, we will investigate some of the most profound criticisms of moral philosophy produced in modernity. We will ask what role, if any, might be left for moral philosophy in their wake? And, what kind of moral philosophy, if any, could one pursue in light of their criticisms?

title: The Symbol, or the Problem of Meaning in the Modern World
description: Explores the modern invention of the symbol, in response to a problem of meaning created by the withdrawal of religious traditions in an increasingly secular world. Beginning with Edgar Allan Poe and ending with Clifford Geertz, we reconstruct the itinerary of the symbol as it passes through literature, philosophy, and anthropology. With one eye cast back on the religious background from which it emerged in nineteenth-century America, we will ask what the symbol inherits from religion, what it replaces but also what it preserves.

title: Toxic Native America
description: An exploration of the contamination of Native American lands with toxic materials and their effect on Native American culture. Explores the concept of wastelanding and the effects that nuclear weapons development, fossil fuel and mineral extraction, mine abandonment, hazardous waste disposal, and other sources of toxic contamination as well as global climate change have on traditional lifeways of diverse Native American communities.
